title: Background & Profile — Pablo Wynistorf
description: Curated background facts about Pablo Wynistorf, compiled from pablo.one and public sources.
text: About Pablo Wynistorf Pablo Wynistorf is an IT Technician from Switzerland who specialises in cloud computing and network infrastructure. He builds projects primarily on Amazon Web Services (AWS) and publishes a portfolio of his work and certifications at pablo.one. Cloud computing & competitions WorldSkills Lyon 2024 — Pablo represented Switzerland in the Cloud Computing skill and was awarded a Medallion for Excellence (September 2024). The competition ran over three days and was carried out exclusively on the AWS platform. WorldSkills Lyon 2024 was the 47th WorldSkills Competition , held at Eurexpo Lyon, France from 10–15 September 2024 — the global championship of vocational skills, with competitors from 80+ countries. In Switzerland the Cloud Computing discipline runs under the Skills53 banner (skills53.ch), the SwissSkills/WorldSkills cloud computing category for IT apprentices, with challenges built on AWS. His WorldSkills preparation began in January 2024 under his coach Pascal Mathis , and included extensive hands-on practice, studying a wide range of AWS services, and taking part in AWS Jam and AWS GameDay sessions and several demo competitions. SwissSkills 2023 — Pablo competed in the Cloud Computing category and reached second place , which earned him an invitation to the selection assessment for the national WorldSkills team. title: How this chat platform works — architecture, data and cost
description: How Pablo's AI chat is built — the AWS architecture, how the data is stored and retrieved, and what it costs per month to run.
text: How this chat is built This chat is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbot that Pablo built himself. It answers questions about him in the first person, grounded in his own content, and cites the pages it drew from. It runs entirely serverless on AWS in the eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) region, and the whole thing is deployed from Terraform with a single terraform apply. Written in one sentence: the visitor's question is turned into a vector, the closest passages from Pablo's website, GitHub and LinkedIn are looked up in Amazon S3 Vectors, and those passages are handed to Amazon Bedrock as context so the model answers from real material instead of improvising. The request path Everything enters through a single Amazon CloudFront distribution, which fans out to two origins. That one distribution is also where the TLS certificate lives, so the custom domain and the certificate are configured in exactly one place. The first origin is an Amazon S3 bucket holding the built frontend. Pablo's chat page is a Next.js 14 App Router application with React and Tailwind CSS, and the page itself is entirely client-side, so Next prerenders it to a plain HTML document at build time. That document plus the hashed JavaScript and CSS assets are uploaded to S3 and served from the edge, cached for one minute. The bucket is private: it has no public access whatsoever and is readable only by CloudFront, through an Origin Access Control signed request. The second origin is an API Gateway HTTP API, reached only through the /api/ path pattern on the same distribution. Behind it sits a single AWS Lambda function on arm64 with 1024 MB of memory, running the Next.js server through the AWS Lambda Web Adapter. That behaviour has caching switched off completely, because answers are streamed and the opening greeting is personalised per visitor. Compression is switched off on that path too — letting the edge compress a streamed response would make it buffer, which would break the token-by-token streaming. Splitting it this way means the Lambda no longer serves static files at all. Every asset request is answered by CloudFront or S3, and the function only ever runs for actual API calls. When someone asks a question, the API route embeds the question with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 into a 1024-dimension vector, queries Amazon S3 Vectors for the nearest passages, assembles them into a prompt, and streams the answer back token by token from Amazon Nova Micro via the Bedrock Converse streaming API. Sources are sent ahead of the answer in a response header so the citation chips can render before the text arrives. How the data is stored Three kinds of storage, each doing one job: an S3 bucket for the built frontend, an S3 Vectors index for everything searchable, and a small DynamoDB table for usage counters. There is no database and no vector database cluster. Everything searchable lives in Amazon S3 Vectors , a purpose-built vector store, in one vector bucket with a single index named pages. The index is configured as float32, 1024 dimensions, cosine distance. The corpus is about 1,956 vectors totalling roughly 11.7 MB. Each vector is one chunk of text and carries the passage itself alongside it as metadata, so a single query returns both the ranking and the material the model needs — there is no second fetch. Prose is chunked into overlapping windows of 220 words with 40 words of overlap; source code uses a line-aligned splitter so functions are not cut mid-body. Metadata is split deliberately. The fields title, text and description are stored and returned but are not filterable. The fields url, section, repo, path and language stay filterable, and that is what makes the retrieval trick work: source code is about 96% of the index, so an unfiltered search returns code for almost any question. Instead the app runs two filtered queries in parallel — one excluding the code section, one containing only it — and blends the results according to whether the question actually looks like it is about code. Four sources feed the index: the pablo.one website discovered through its sitemap, public GitHub repositories with their READMEs, the actual source files from those repositories, and hand-written markdown notes for things that cannot be crawled. LinkedIn blocks automated crawling and returns HTTP 999 to bots, so the LinkedIn content is a curated file rather than a scrape. A small Amazon DynamoDB table tracks usage: the running AI spend per day and a per-IP message count. Every item has a TTL so the counters clean themselves up after about two days. Nothing about visitors is stored beyond those counters. Safety and cost controls An Amazon Bedrock Guardrail restricts the conversation to topics about Pablo, so off-topic questions and prompt-injection attempts get a polite refusal. A daily budget cap converts the real token usage of every model call into micro-dollars and accumulates it in DynamoDB; once the day's spend reaches the configured limit the chat stops generating and the greeting falls back to a static message. There is also a per-IP daily message limit and a maximum length per message, both rejected before any model call is made. All of these fail open: if the tracking table is unreachable the chat still works. What it costs to run per month Every component is usage-based, so the bill scales with traffic and there is no idle cost. There is no NAT gateway, no load balancer, no always-on search cluster and no managed database — the things that normally dominate an AWS bill are simply absent. The unit prices in eu-central-1 are: AWS Lambda on arm64 at $0.0000133334 per GB-second and $0.20 per million requests; API Gateway HTTP API at $1.20 per million requests; Nova Micro at $0.000035 per thousand input tokens and $0.00014 per thousand output tokens; Titan Text Embeddings V2 at $0.0002 per thousand tokens; and S3 Vectors at $0.064 per GB-month of storage plus $0.214 per GB written. At the traffic a personal portfolio actually gets — on the order of a few hundred visits and a few hundred chat messages a month — the total lands at roughly 10 to 20 US cents per month . Storing the entire vector index costs about $0.0007 per month, or seven hundredths of a cent. A few hundred chat messages cost around five cents in Bedrock tokens. API Gateway adds under a cent. The daily AI budget cap means model spend cannot exceed about $15 in a month even under sustained abuse, and the per-IP message limit makes reaching that ceiling difficult in the first place. For comparison, the obvious managed alternatives would cost far more while sitting idle: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Aurora Serverless both bill for provisioned capacity whether or not anyone runs a query, which is the wrong shape entirely for a site that might get a handful of visits a day. That trade-off is the main reason the project uses S3 Vectors. Chromium's high-entropy Client Hints are requested with an Accept-CH header so details like the exact browser version and platform are available; because the document is served from S3, which cannot return arbitrary headers, that header is added by a CloudFront response headers policy at the edge. Location comes from a keyless IP geolocation lookup, capped by a short timeout and cached per address for six hours. CloudFront can also attach headers describing the viewer's city, country, timezone and network, and the code prefers those when present — but they are not switched on here. Those headers are only accepted in a CloudFront origin request policy, and such a policy is limited to ten headers in total, which is not enough room to also forward the Content-Type, User-Agent, Accept-Language and Client Hint headers the API actually needs. Breaking the JSON request to avoid one cached lookup would be a poor trade. Every one of those values is treated as untrusted input, sanitised and bounded before it goes anywhere near the model prompt. The interface shows its own working through a "How did I know that?" panel under the greeting. Deployment Terraform provisions everything: the vector bucket and index, the frontend bucket, the CloudFront distribution, the guardrail, the usage table, the IAM roles, the Lambda function and the API Gateway. It also runs the build itself and uploads the result, so one terraform apply takes the project from an empty account to a working, populated chatbot. The build runs as a Terraform external data source rather than a provisioner. That is deliberate: the S3 upload manages every file as an individual Terraform resource, and Terraform resolves those at plan time, so the built files have to exist before planning begins. A provisioner only runs during apply, which would be too late on a fresh clone. The build stamps a hash of its inputs and skips itself when nothing changed, so repeated plans stay fast. Uploading through managed resources rather than a sync command means Terraform can show exactly which assets change, and deleting a source file deletes the object. A new build also triggers a CloudFront invalidation, because the HTML document keeps the same name while its contents change.
